title: Keeping girls in secondary school
summary: A small local education charity works in a rural district where girls leave secondary school earlier than boys. It tackles four reasons together: cost, unsafe journeys, expectations at home, and how quickly schools respond when a girl starts missing class.
whyThisWorks: The problem statement says who is affected, how much and why, without naming the project. Each activity answers one of the stated reasons. Outputs are things the charity delivers and can count directly. Outcomes are changes in attendance and behaviour that it influences but doesn't control. The assumptions name what else must hold true, such as schools having enough places for larger classes.

items: In a rural district, 38% of girls who enrol in secondary school leave before finishing lower secondary, compared with 21% of boys. Families cite the cost of fees, uniforms and transport. Girls describe the walk to school as unsafe, and household work increases as they get older.
assumptions: School enrolment and attendance records are complete enough to show the gap between girls and boys.

indicators.text: Share of girls enrolled in Year 7 who are still enrolled in Year 9
indicators.target: Tracked for context. Targets are set at outcome and impact level.

items: Provide bursaries covering fees, uniforms and materials for the 300 girls most at risk of leaving, selected with schools and community leaders
Organise supervised walking groups and a bicycle-loan scheme for girls who live more than 3 km from school
Run termly sessions with parents and caregivers on the value of finishing secondary school and on sharing household tasks
Train 40 teachers in gender-responsive teaching and in spotting early signs that a pupil may drop out
assumptions: Schools agree to share attendance data every month.
Funding arrives in time to pay bursaries before each term starts.

indicators.text: Number of girls whose bursary is paid before the start of term

items: 300 girls a year receive full bursaries before term starts
Safe-travel schemes run on 6 routes, used by up to 150 girls
12 caregiver sessions held each year, reaching 400 caregivers
40 teachers trained and using an early-warning attendance checklist
assumptions: Girls and caregivers take up the offer, and bursaries carry no stigma.
Trained teachers stay in their posts.

indicators.text: Number of trained teachers returning the early-warning checklist each month
indicators.target: 35 of 40 by the end of year 1

items: Cost is no longer the main reason families give for keeping girls at home
Teachers act early when a girl's attendance drops
assumptions: No sharp rise in other household costs, such as food prices, pushes girls into paid work.

indicators.text: Average attendance rate of girls in participating schools
indicators.meansOfVerification: School attendance registers, checked each term

items: More girls move from Year 7 to Year 9 without leaving school
Caregivers expect and plan for their daughters to finish lower secondary
assumptions: Schools have enough places and teachers for larger Year 8 and Year 9 classes.
Pressure for early marriage does not increase in the district.

indicators.text: Share of girls enrolled in Year 7 who are still enrolled in Year 9
indicators.meansOfVerification: School enrolment records, checked yearly with the district education office

items: Girls in the district finish lower secondary school at the same rate as boys
assumptions: The government keeps funding secondary schools in the district.

indicators.text: Gap between girls' and boys' lower-secondary completion rates

draftPairs.improved: 300 girls a year receive full bursaries before term starts
draftPairs.why: Better attendance is a change in behaviour, so it belongs under outcomes. An output is something the project delivers and can count directly.

draftPairs.improved: Girls in the district finish lower secondary school at the same rate as boys
draftPairs.why: The first version is too broad to measure or to link back to the activities. The improved version names one specific change that can be observed.
